name: Gareth Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most mornings I'm at the city hospital or the housing office by nine, interpreting French for patients and tenants, mostly people from West and Central Africa. The agency books me in two-hour slots and pays per slot, so a cancelled appointment is money gone. Afternoons I sit at the kitchen table in our rented flat and translate letters, school reports and tenancy papers, with my paper glossary next to me. Ama, my partner, works shifts at a pharmacy, so some days we only see each other at breakfast.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment a scared patient realises someone in the room actually understands them. That's why I took this up. What wears me out is the paperwork side: agencies cutting the rate for written work every year and telling me the machine already did half of it. I've never used those tools, and I'm still slow on medical terms, so I lose evenings checking words my mentor Pierre would know straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. People at the agency have been saying the machines would replace us for three years, and here we'd be with patients still needing a person beside them. Online I'd probably share something from the translators' guild about fair rates, because the rate problem doesn't go away just because the hype does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't mean I'm safe. The agencies already use machine translation as an excuse to pay me less for written work, and even a small dent in routine letters hits me because that's half my income. The interpreting would carry on, but I'd still be a junior on two-hour slots with no sick pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the hospital and housing slots and try to get more of them, maybe ask for the Tuesday clinic that Pierre is giving up. I'd sit the community interpreting exam next spring, which costs about four hundred, so I can charge more. And I'd keep my two months of savings where they are and not touch them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly tired, I think. Even the boring version has me fighting for every slot and every cent a word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the rate problem doesn't go away. What does that look like in a normal month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last March the agency dropped written work from twelve cents a word to nine and called it post-editing, which means fixing what a machine wrote. I did the maths at the kitchen table with Ama and it was about two hundred less a month for the same hours. Our rent is due on the first and my income lands whenever clients pay, so some months I'm borrowing from her until the fifteenth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about that, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guild, and Pierre. Pierre's been interpreting for twenty years and he says rates only held when people stuck together and refused the worst jobs. I've been to two guild meetings and I'd go to more, even if it's mostly older people complaining in a church hall.

say: I'd say the **hype was wrong** and patients still need a real person in the room.
I'd share the guild's posts about **fair rates**, because the pay squeeze carries on regardless.
think: Even a small machine dent hits me, because **written work** is half my income.
I'd still be a **junior on slots** with no sick pay and lumpy months.
do: Ask for the **Tuesday clinic** slots that Pierre, his mentor, is giving up.
Sit the **interpreting exam** next spring for about four hundred, to charge more.
Leave his **two months of savings** untouched.
feel: Mostly **tired** of fighting for every slot and every cent a word.
S0.quote: The agency dropped written work from twelve cents a word to nine and called it post-editing, which means fixing what a machine wrote.
fieldNote: He already feels the **rate squeeze** even in the calm picture, so calm didn't fit.
His comfort comes from the **hospital work**, where a person in the room still matters.
Leans on **Pierre and the guild** rather than tools; he's never tried machine translation himself.

steps.text: Take on the Tuesday hospital clinic slots Pierre is giving up
Sit the community interpreting exam next spring for about four hundred
Go to the translators' guild meetings about fair rates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say what the guild says: the agencies are using software to cut corners on people's health and housing. I'd post about a hospital letter getting a dosage wrong, because I think that would happen. I'd be loud about it, more than usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the written half of my income disappears within two years in that picture. Letters, school reports, tenancy papers, that's exactly the checking and writing it describes. The interpreting would hold longer, but even there the hospital would try tablets with an app first, and I'm the junior, so I'm the first one they stop booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop chasing written work and push hard for interpreting hours, even evenings and weekends at the police station. I'd ask Ama if we could move somewhere cheaper when the lease ends in August. I'd join the guild properly, pay the eighty a year, and sign whatever they send to the health board about keeping human interpreters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. I spent four years learning French grammar to be told a phone does it fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop chasing written work. Would you ever learn the tools instead, the way some translators do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ama asked me the same thing. I know I probably should, but I don't trust them, and I'd be learning to do the job that's replacing me for less money. Maybe I'd try once if the guild ran a course, but I'm not going to be the person checking a machine at nine cents a word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ama about money that month the written work stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we'd have to live on her pharmacy pay plus whatever slots I get, and that the savings are for rent only. We've talked about a holiday in Lisbon next summer, and that would be the first thing to go. She'd be fine about it, she always is, which somehow makes it worse.

say: I'd say agencies are **cutting corners** on people's health and housing with software.
I'd post about a **wrong dosage** in a hospital letter, because I expect that to happen.
think: The **written half** of my income goes within two years in this picture.
Even interpreting slips, because the **junior is dropped** first when tablets come in.
do: Push for **interpreting hours**, including evenings at the police station.
Ask Ama to **move somewhere cheaper** when the lease ends in August.
Pay the **guild's eighty a year** and sign its letter to the health board.
feel: **Sick** that four years of French grammar might count for little.
S1.quote: I spent four years learning French grammar to be told a phone does it fine.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose half his income** quickly, so the mood is alarmed, not anxious.
Refuses to **learn the tools**, partly on principle and partly from distrust.
Leans on his partner's **pharmacy pay**; the cancelled Lisbon trip shows the squeeze.

steps.text: Switch from written jobs to police station and hospital interpreting
Join the translators' guild and sign its letter to the health board
Move to a cheaper flat with Ama when the lease ends in August
Cancel the Lisbon holiday planned for next summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need laws before it lands, not after. At the hospital I'd tell the nurses that someone has to be legally responsible when the machine gets a consent form wrong. Online I'd be angry, probably angrier than is good for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I'm finished as a translator by 2028 in that one. My whole job is thinking work, words in and words out, so I don't even get the three extra years the plumbers get. Maybe the hospital keeps a few human interpreters for difficult cases, but those would go to Pierre and the senior people, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before it lands, I'd use the two years to train for something with my hands, maybe as a healthcare assistant, since I already know the wards. I'd keep interpreting while it lasts and put every spare bit into savings to get past three months. Once it arrives, I'd lean on Ama and on whatever support the government sets up, and I'd be at every guild meeting pushing for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'm twenty-seven and the one thing I trained for would be gone before I got good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the plumbers get three more years. Does the robot part change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for the plan B. If I go into care work on the wards, I've maybe got until 2031 before a robot can lift a patient, and that's not long either. I'd still do it, because three years of wages is three years, and I think people will want a person holding their hand longer than the robots are ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum paid for my year in Lyon, so that conversation would be hard. I'd tell my mum the degree wasn't wasted, that it got me into the hospital and taught me how to listen to frightened people. I'm not sure I'd believe it while saying it.

say: I'd say we need **laws first**, with someone legally responsible for machine errors.
I'd be **angry online**, probably angrier than is good for me.
think: My job is all **thinking work**, so I don't get the robots' three-year delay.
The few **hard cases** left would go to senior interpreters, not me.
do: Train as a **healthcare assistant** on the wards he already knows.
Save every spare bit to get **past three months** of expenses.
Lean on Ama and **government support** once it arrives, and push the guild.
feel: **Frightened** that his training goes before he even got good at it.
S2.quote: I'm twenty-seven and the one thing I trained for would be gone before I got good at it.
fieldNote: He clearly sees his job as **pure thinking work** with no hands-on buffer.
His fallback is **care work**, which buys him roughly until the robots in 2031.
Calls for **laws and support** fit his progressive views; he doesn't blame the patients or nurses.

steps.text: Train as a healthcare assistant on the hospital wards
Save every spare bit until savings pass three months
Lean on Ama's pay and any new government support
Push the guild to campaign for laws on machine errors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing as the fast one, just with more time to organise. I'd be telling the guild to get in front of the health board now while there's still a debate. Five years is enough to win something if people move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is a mixed bag for me. Five years is enough time to get qualified at something else, but not enough for translation to be worth the effort of getting better at. So I'd be half in, half out of a job I chose on purpose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit the interpreting exam anyway, because it'd lift my rate for the years I've got left. Then from year two I'd start a part-time nursing course in the evenings, which is about three years. Ama and I would hold off on buying a place and keep renting, so the savings stay ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, then sad, then a bit angry. It's like watching a train come down the line you're standing on, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why nursing, rather than care assistant work like you said before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I could afford the longer course, and nurses do the hands-on work and the judgement. I know that thinking part will go too, but the robots come three years after, so a nurse in 2031 still has years of lifting and dressing. Pierre's daughter is a nurse, and she says they're short everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to pay for evening classes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Football on Saturdays, probably, and the takeaway on Fridays. The course fees would come out of my interpreting money, so I'd take every police station call-out I could get. I wouldn't touch the savings unless something went really wrong.

say: I'd tell the guild to **organise now** while there's still a public debate.
I'd say five years is enough to **win something** if people move together.
think: Five years is enough to **requalify**, but not to make translation worth it.
I'd feel **half in, half out** of a job I chose on purpose.
do: Sit the **interpreting exam** to lift his rate for the years left.
Start a **part-time nursing course** in the evenings from year two.
Keep renting and hold off **buying a place**.
feel: **Uneasy, then sad**, like watching a slow train come down his line.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to get qualified at something else, but not enough for translation to be worth the effort of getting better at.
fieldNote: The extra time turns him from **care assistant to nurse**, a longer and better-paid route.
He still expects to **lose translation income**, so the mood stays alarmed.
Cuts are small and **personal**: football and Friday takeaways.

steps.text: Start a part-time nursing course in evenings from year two
Drop Saturday football and Friday takeaways to pay course fees
Keep renting with Ama instead of buying a flat
Press the guild to lobby the health board now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got ten years, so there's no excuse for anyone being left behind. I'd want the guild and the health service planning retraining now, paid for properly. I'd say it calmly for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years helps me more than almost anyone, because I'm young. I could become a full nurse, work a few years, and still be under forty when the robots arrive. The translation part of my life would end, but I wouldn't be ruined by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep interpreting for three or four more years and get good at it, since it pays the bills meanwhile. I'd do the nursing degree part-time from 2028, and maybe Ama and I would think about having a child once I've qualified. I'd still put a bit aside each month, maybe a hundred, for the gap years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others, though not happy. There's grief in it, but there's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said translation would end. Is there any part of it you'd fight to keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hospital interpreting, at least for the hardest conversations, like telling someone their child is very ill. I don't think a family wants a screen for that. But I'm realistic. In ten years the machine might be gentler with a frightened family than I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Ama know you're thinking about nursing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mentioned it once and she laughed and said I'd faint at blood. I wouldn't faint. Probably.

say: I'd say ten years means **no excuse** for leaving anyone behind.
I'd want **paid retraining** planned now by the guild and health service.
think: Being young, a decade lets me **become a nurse** and still be under forty.
Translation would end, but I **wouldn't be ruined** by it.
do: Keep **interpreting** for three or four years to pay the bills.
Put aside about **a hundred a month** for the gap years.
feel: **Calmer** than the other pictures, though grieving, because there's a plan.
S4.quote: In ten years the machine might be gentler with a frightened family than I am.
fieldNote: Ten years flips his view: being **young** becomes an advantage.
Still expects to **lose the job**, so anxious rather than calm.
He'd hold on to the **hardest hospital talks** as the human part worth keeping.

steps.text: Start a part-time nursing degree from 2028
Put aside about a hundred a month for the gap years
Plan a child with Ama once his nursing degree is done
Campaign for paid retraining through the guild and health service

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, by a mile, because I'd be out before I'd built anything else. What would help is the health service paying for interpreters to retrain as nurses or care staff, with a wage while we train. Even six months of support would change everything for someone like me with two months saved.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be told you're replaceable by people who don't speak the language. The managers who book me can't tell if a translation is good or terrible. If AI does take this work, I'd like at least one person who speaks French to check it before a patient signs something.

headlineQuote: The managers who book me can't tell if a translation is good or terrible.
portrait: A **27-year-old** French–English interpreter on two-hour hospital and housing slots, living with his partner Ama.
Never uses **AI tools** and distrusts them; leans on his mentor Pierre and the guild.
Already feels a **rate squeeze**, so even AI Plateau leaves him uneasy.
Expects to **lose written work** fast in Steady Disruption and plans a switch to nursing in the AGI pictures.
Ten years feels **survivable** to him because he's young enough to start again.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be out before building anything else.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** into nursing or care, with a wage while training.
A **French speaker** checking machine translations before patients sign anything.
